a294.speaker: Libyan Ministry of the Interior (statement published on Facebook)
a294.speech: Reported the apprehension of 87 irregular migrants, originating from various African countries, in the course of a series of security operations conducted in the vicinity of Ghadames, a border region of western Libya close to Algeria ; specified that border guard units, attached to the Ghadames security sector, had patrolled desert areas, valleys and unpaved tracks leading to the town ; stressed that these actions form part of a reinforced surveillance plan deployed by the security services responsible for border control in south-western Libya.

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement addressed to Governor Dauda Lawal)
a509.speech: Decried what it described as the "appalling condition" of the school, calling on the governor to urgently address what it termed a humanitarian and governance failure: "The appalling condition of UBE Low-Cost Primary School in Gusau Tudun Wada Ward, Gusau LGA, Zamfara State, paints a grim picture of the state of basic education in Zamfara."

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement)
a509.speech: Stated that over 113 children in the school are currently learning in distressing conditions, sitting on bare floors without desks, chairs, or a conducive learning environment, and that overcrowded classrooms have made learning nearly impossible: "Many classrooms are so overcrowded that two classes are merged into one, making effective teaching and learning almost impossible. For many of these children, learning happens while seated on dusty floors in deteriorating classrooms, a situation that denies them the most basic dignity and comfort that education should guarantee."

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement)
a509.speech: Expressed dismay that such conditions persist despite the huge sums allocated to education in successive state budgets: "This disturbing reality persists despite the repeated promises and substantial budgets announced by the Zamfara State Government. In the recently presented N545 billion 2025 'Rescue Budget 2.0', Governor Dauda Lawal allocated 14% (N79.6 billion) to the education sector." ; "Similarly, the 2024 budget of N426 billion, signed into law earlier this year, earmarked N51.3 billion for education."

a509.speaker: Zamfara State Government (as quoted in the statement)
a509.speech: "The government has consistently emphasized that these budgets are designed to 'address pressing needs' and 'advance critical infrastructure' in schools."

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement)
a509.speech: Noted that Zamfara continues to benefit from federal and international interventions aimed at improving education: "Zamfara State also continues to receive federal allocations through the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), as well as substantial support from international partners, including UNICEF, USAID, and the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), all aimed at strengthening basic education." ; "However, the impact of these funds is nowhere to be seen in schools like UBE Low-Cost Primary School, where pupils endure conditions unfit for learning in the 21st century."

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement)
a509.speech: Accused the government of misplaced spending priorities: "While pupils are sitting on the ground in underfunded classrooms, the same state government reportedly spent N974 million on foreign trips, money that could have equipped thousands of classrooms, provided basic furniture, and improved the learning environment for children across Zamfara."

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement)
a509.speech: Described the situation as a "failure of governance, accountability, and political will," warning that continued neglect could jeopardize Zamfara's human capital development: "The situation at UBE Low-Cost Primary School is not just a reflection of underdevelopment; it is a failure of governance, accountability, and political will. It highlights the widening gap between the billions allocated to education on paper and the harsh realities faced by children in public schools." ; "Education is not a privilege; it is a fundamental right and the foundation of human capital development." ; "The current state of Zamfara's public schools is a direct violation of that right. It is unacceptable that in 2025, with billions budgeted and multiple streams of domestic and international support, children still learn while sitting on bare floors."

a509.speaker: MonITNG (civic accountability platform, statement)
a509.speech: Concluded by urging Governor Lawal to act decisively, "declare a state of emergency in education and ensure that budgeted funds truly reach classrooms. Zamfara's future depends on it".

a737.speaker: Apollinaire Bangayimbaga, Rector of the University of Ngozi
a737.speech: In his welcoming remarks, hailed the good relations existing between the University of Ngozi and the United States Embassy in Burundi. He said that the centre helps students with capacity building and with research, and that it also provides internet access and programmes that help young people build their future. He then thanked the United States Embassy in Burundi, which, through USAID, helped the University of Ngozi set up a laboratory that assists with research and with the promotion of agriculture.

a737.speaker: Amy Davison, Deputy Chief of Mission at the United States Embassy in Burundi
a737.speech: Indicated that the American Corner centres in Burundi play an essential role as a dynamic platform for promoting educational opportunities, civic engagement and cultural exchange among young Burundians. She stressed that these centres are genuine catalysts of change for Burundian youth, while offering a safe, inclusive and stimulating space where young people can learn and commit to opening themselves to the world. Congratulating the certified graduates, she specified that English is a lever of social transformation, a dominant tool for research and a bridge to the world; for her, mastery of English fosters the exchange of experiences and also makes it possible to discover different cultural perspectives.

a798.speaker: Dispatch/news release from Rome, Italy
a798.speech: According to a dispatch, the conversation between President Boakai and the Executive Chairman of ArcelorMittal focused on crucial transformative programs, including but not limited to strengthening economic ties and making intentional investment in youth development; a news release from Rome reported that President Joseph Boakai held a crucial discussion with Mr. Lakshmi N. Mittal.

a798.speaker: Lakshmi N. Mittal, Executive Chairman of ArcelorMittal
a798.speech: Reaffirmed long-standing commitment to Liberia's economic development; highlighted the shared vision of the company and the government for the country's future, stating ArcelorMittal will remain one of Liberia's most significant industrial partners; also emphasized the company's deep connection to Liberia and its strategic importance in Liberia's economic landscape ; "ArcelorMittal's activities are not only essential to the country's current economic framework, but they are pivotal for the future vision of Liberia" ; reiterated that ArcelorMittal's investment in Liberia is a long-term partnership aimed at fostering sustainable development, and during an earlier visit reinforced ArcelorMittal's commitment to expanding its operations in Liberia and continuing its investment in the country's infrastructure, particularly in the mining sector.

a798.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a798.speech: Acknowledged the significant contributions of foreign investors like ArcelorMittal, not only to the economy but to Liberia's broader development goals; praised ArcelorMittal for its role as a model investor, calling current investors "ambassadors" for others considering doing business in Liberia ; "Investors like ArcelorMittal are not only contributing to our economy but are helping to shape the future of our nation by supporting the training and development of young Liberians"

a798.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a798.speech: Emphasized that investing in youth training and development is crucial to Liberia's long-term growth, and that foreign partners like ArcelorMittal play an essential role in this effort ; "Our youth need the skills and training to step into leadership and make meaningful contributions to national development. This is an area where ArcelorMittal's involvement is invaluable"

a950.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) (joint statement)
a950.speech: have committed to deepening their collaboration for displaced people and host communities in South Sudan; highlighted investments in refugee and returnee areas and the local communities hosting them, as well as the crucial role of partnerships between humanitarian and development actors.

a950.speaker: Raouf Mazou, UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Operations
a950.speech: “South Sudan has generously kept its border open to receive people fleeing the war in Sudan, but they can't do it alone. More humanitarian and development support is needed to deliver life-saving assistance and enable conflict-affected communities to get back on their feet and rebuild their lives,” Mazou said in a joint statement issued in Juba.

a950.speaker: UNHCR
a950.speech: According to the UNHCR, more than half a million people have arrived in South Sudan since the start of the war in Sudan on April 15, 2023, most of them South Sudanese who had been in Sudan for decades; it said many people are heading back to villages that barely have any services, where there is no humanitarian assistance available; the UNHCR said the Sudanese refugees are being relocated to refugee settlements where resources were already overstretched.

a950.speaker: Marie-Laure Akin-Olugbade, AfDB Vice President for Regional Development, Integration, and Business Delivery
a950.speech: said they are committed to responding to the biggest development challenges facing the African continent, including preventing and addressing forced displacement ; “Our collaboration and partnership with the UNHCR is an important and critical way to advance resilience and durable solutions for refugees, IDPs (internally displaced persons), returnees, and host communities in South Sudan.”

a950.speaker: High-level South Sudanese government officials
a950.speech: welcomed the partnership and collaboration addressing the pressing needs in the country.

a1100.speaker: Pr Moussa Hamidou Talibi, Secretary General of the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Technological Innovation of Niger, representing the minister
a1100.speech: "This flagship activity, organised every two years by these two important institutions, is one of the privileged platforms offered to academics, researchers and scholars to exchange on questions and challenges affecting our world, especially in conflict zones where the behaviour of terrorists towards civilians increasingly constitutes a problem that calls out to all humanity," declared at the opening of the colloquium's work ; "International humanitarian law (IHL), which governs relations between men in time of war, faces immense challenges that call out to us all," noting that Islamic law "reflects better than anything else our spiritual and religious values" ; "The protection of populations and the prohibition on attacking their means of survival, coupled with the obligation to bring them relief and assistance, are profoundly Islamic values, and it is in this that IHL draws largely on Islam and is nourished by it."

a1100.speaker: Pr Moussa Hamidou Talibi, Secretary General of the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Technological Innovation of Niger, representing the minister
a1100.speech: Said this year's theme on the protection of populations comes "at the right time in a Sahelian context marked by the spread of terrorism which affects, first and foremost, the labouring masses, and this trend should be reversed by the commitment of all to uphold the principles of law and respect for human dignity, both in time of peace and in time of conflict" ; "Niger, a signatory of the Geneva Conventions, encourages this kind of scientific meeting and urges public as well as private universities to join this logic," welcomed the ministry's representative, recalling that Niger "has always been one of the models in respecting human dignity and hence in observing the rules of IHL" ; "It is with this in mind that the CNSP and the government are doing everything to make the defence and protection of our populations effective, not only in the field of security, but also in the basic social sectors, and strongly encourage this kind of meeting which makes it possible to deepen reflection with a view to achieving greater protection for our populations who aspire to tranquillity and development in a world of peace," he concluded.

a1100.speaker: Christoph Vogt, head of the ICRC delegation in Niger
a1100.speech: "This impressive attendance and the quality of the participants testify to the importance you attach to the issues we are submitting for debate, with a view to bringing out and highlighting the many points of convergence between Islamic law and international humanitarian law (IHL), often also rightly called the international law of armed conflict." ; explained that the colloquium on the protection of civilian populations in IHL and in Islamic law (Fiqh) "is being held in a global context marked by the multiplication and recurrence of armed conflicts with their toll of victims, especially among civilian populations who, often direct victims of hostilities, can also be indirect victims of them, through the destruction of infrastructure indispensable to their survival" ; said that in most armed conflicts "millions of people also flee their lands to escape war and its violence, and by targeting civilians the belligerents violate IHL and all the other protective norms, including Islamic law", noting that consequently civilian victims find themselves in a situation of extreme precariousness and vulnerability and become totally dependent on the assistance of States and humanitarian aid ; "For the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, the protection of civilians in armed conflicts covers activities aimed at ensuring full respect for the rights of persons not participating, or no longer participating, in hostilities."

a1100.speaker: Dr A. Razak Tchoussou, Vice-Rector of the Islamic University of Niger
a1100.speech: Recalled that "the Islamic University in Niger and the ICRC have a tradition, that of organising together each year a series of conferences and every two years a regional colloquium on questions of humanitarian law and Islamic law" ; said this year's colloquium theme, "beyond falling within the secular humanitarian mission of the ICRC and of Islam, finds all its importance in the current regional security context, where the target populations are at the centre of the concerns of the various public authorities" ; said that in "the current global, regional and sub-regional context, characterised by the direct exposure of populations to conflicts and the consequences of these conflicts, this colloquium, through the different themes that will be addressed by our eminent speakers bringing together scientists, experts in the humanitarian field, ulemas and scholars of Islamic law from several countries, is a unique opportunity to enable participants to understand, master and appropriate the different tools for protecting target populations".

a1100.speaker: Dr A. Razak Tchoussou, Vice-Rector of the Islamic University of Niger
a1100.speech: Saluted the President of the CNSP, Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani, and Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine for "all the efforts in favour of the protection and securing of our populations, and the Minister of Higher Education, Research and Technological Innovation, Professor Saidou Mamadou, who spares no effort to steer higher education towards excellence and whose actions and advice have always been precious for the Islamic University in Niger".

a1104.speaker: African Private Capital Association (AVCA)
a1104.speech: Announced Lagos as the host city for the AVCA Annual Conference and Venture Capital Summit in 2025.

a1104.speaker: Panellists at the 3rd Annual AVCA Venture Capital Summit
a1104.speech: Took stock of the global decline of VC funding and explored a range of solutions to catalyse growth ; speakers marked the influence of rapidly emerging technologies shaping African innovation and driving the digital economy, creating new skills and increasing efficiency, such as artificial intelligence, blockchain and quantum computing.

a1104.speaker: Andre Jr. Ayotte, Partner, Modus Capital
a1104.speech: Speaking on the panel 'The DeepTech Potential in African Tech', highlighted how founders can apply technology to build companies solving problems at scale.

a1104.speaker: Nick Allen, Managing Partner, Savant
a1104.speech: Noted that gaps in Africa's tertiary education system have led to a lack of skilled graduates with sufficient engineering knowledge; added that in comparison to more developed markets such as Europe and the US, there is a lack of investors who understand how to finance deep tech in Africa.

a1104.speaker: Khaled Ben Jilani, Senior Partner, AfricInvest
a1104.speech: Raised the importance of active strategies to make businesses less capital intensive in order to anticipate new risks and navigate a lack of liquidity in the market.

a1104.speaker: Steve Beck, Co-Founder and Managing Partner, Novastar Ventures
a1104.speech: Expressed that private equity firms and development finance institutions (DFIs) with dedicated VC teams had stepped in to partially fill the funding gaps, particularly in the early stages.

a1173.speaker: United Nations (recent reports)
a1173.speech: In 2024, around 7.1 million people in Mali need humanitarian assistance, that is nearly 30% of the population, a figure confirmed by recent United Nations reports.

a1173.speaker: Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations
a1173.speech: At a recent donors' conference held in Saudi Arabia, reiterated the importance of increased international aid for the populations of the Sahel, whose development potential is immense despite the current challenges.

a1274.speaker: Attahiru Bafarawa, former Sokoto State governor
a1274.speech: has urged President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to allow opposition politics to flourish, warning that stifling dissent could harm democracy and national development. In an open letter on Monday, Bafarawa reminded Tinubu that his own rise to power was made possible by a thriving opposition. "Those before you allowed opposition politics to exist. You are a product of opposition politics. It would be a grave mistake to suppress it now." ; "Anyone advising you to muzzle the opposition is misleading you. Democracy dies where opposition is stifled, and without democracy, good governance, peace, and progress suffer." ; He cautioned Tinubu against discarding the democratic system that enabled his ascent, warning that silencing opposition voices would tarnish his reputation.

a1274.speaker: Attahiru Bafarawa, former Sokoto State governor
a1274.speech: also warned against attempts to create a one-party state, calling it a dangerous path that could lead to instability. "Nigeria cannot afford a one-party system. A strong democratic order is essential for national progress and for future generations."

a1274.speaker: Attahiru Bafarawa, former Sokoto State governor
a1274.speech: urged Tinubu to emulate the United States, where two dominant parties sustain democracy. "If past leaders had destroyed the opposition, you wouldn't have had a platform to reach your current position. Rather than weaken the opposition, it would be wiser to institutionalise strong political parties." ; He concluded by urging Tinubu to uphold democratic principles, calling it the greatest legacy he could leave behind.

a1380.speaker: Somali authorities and humanitarian agencies
a1380.speech: According to authorities and humanitarian agencies, at least 17 people have died across Somalia due to flash flooding caused by seasonal Gu rains (April–June), which began in mid-April and have since inundated southern and central parts of the country.

a1380.speaker: Banadir Regional Administration
a1380.speech: Confirmed that 11 of the fatalities occurred in Mogadishu, where heavy rainfall on May 9–10 led to widespread damage ; reported extensive damage from the recent floods in Mogadishu, including the submergence of at least 200 houses and damage to nine roads.

a1380.speaker: Banadir officials
a1380.speech: Have issued an urgent appeal for humanitarian assistance for displaced and affected communities.

a1380.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a1380.speech: Reported that more than 84,000 people have been affected nationwide, though some areas remain dry—particularly in Puntland and Somaliland—where drought conditions continue to impact pasture and water availability.

a1380.speaker: Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) Cluster
a1380.speech: Assessments in Mogadishu's Kahda and Daynile districts found that flash floods affected over 3,810 households (approximately 22,500 people), displacing 430 households (2,580 people).

a1380.speaker: UNHCR Protection and Solutions Monitoring Network (PSMN)
a1380.speech: According to the network, approximately 16,200 people in Jowhar were impacted, including displaced persons whose shelters and sanitation facilities were destroyed.

a1380.speaker: Hirshabelle State authorities
a1380.speech: Said floods displaced at least 1,450 households (8,700 people) in Jowhar IDP camps and another 620 households (3,720 people) in Balcad.

a1380.speaker: Health officials at Gaalkacyo South Referral Hospital
a1380.speech: Have recorded a rise in suspected Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD)/cholera cases, with 22 patients currently admitted.

a1380.speaker: Local authorities and humanitarian partners in Buurdhuubo (Jubaland)
a1380.speech: Reported that 3,740 households were affected, with shelters of over 2,000 households severely damaged.

a1380.speaker: Humanitarian partners (Somaliland)
a1380.speech: Partners report that rains in Somaliland have been minimal and below normal.

a1380.speaker: FAO Somalia Water and Land Information Management (SWALIM) unit
a1380.speech: According to the unit, rainfall is expected to decrease in the coming days, with only light showers forecasted for Lower Juba, Hiraan, and Mudug; most of Puntland, Somaliland, and parts of central and southern Somalia are expected to remain dry.

a1380.speaker: Humanitarian partners
a1380.speech: Warn that immediate support is critical for those displaced or affected by the flooding.

a1674.speaker: Maite Nkoana-Mashabane, South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation
a1674.speech: "This is a joint bi-lateral commission, so regularly we will look at things that neighbours look at," she said after the conclusion of the Joint Bilateral Commission for Cooperation with the Kingdom of Lesotho. "The overarching objective of the [Joint Bilateral Commission for Cooperation (JBCC)] is essentially to consolidate not only the historical and cultural ties that exist between South Africa and Lesotho, but also to enhance bilateral cooperation between the two countries." ; "Our commonalities do not end only with language, geography and culture, but our destiny, development and hopes are inextricably intertwined, hence our common resolve to continue working together for the emancipation of our people."

a1674.speaker: Mohlabi Kenneth Tsekoa, Lesotho's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Relations
a1674.speech: Declared that there was a special kind of unity between the two countries. "Lesotho and South Africa have been one from time immemorial."

a1674.speaker: Mohlabi Kenneth Tsekoa, Lesotho's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Relations
a1674.speech: In October last year, complained that previous JBCC agreements signed between Lesotho and South Africa had not been effective, owing to "ailing relations between Lesotho and South Africa".

a1674.speaker: Maite Nkoana-Mashabane, South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation
a1674.speech: "Today's focus was equally on increased bilateral trade and investment and what we need to do to ease cross-border movement." When pushed on what exactly the discussions on cross-border movement entailed, she said one of the key issues raised at these meetings was "securitisation". She said that her counterpart had reassured her that "they [would] be using documents that are verifiable and identifiable". "We've also said that the Kingdom of Lesotho government confirmed that they are finalising their population registry. They are finalising the production of their documents, [and] we will also be working together with our custom officials to respect these documents and handle them with care." ; "From both sides, that our people are going to be treated with respect when they present themselves at the customs gates, so we continue to facilitate this movement of goods, services but above all, people."

a1674.speaker: Jacob Zuma, President of South Africa
a1674.speech: Was quoted at the time as saying, "Many criminals with Lesotho passports have been arrested in South Africa."

a1674.speaker: Thomas Thabane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a1674.speech: When he met with President Zuma last October, he said he had pleaded with the South African president to remove all obstacles "hampering the ease of movement between the two countries". "I emphasised the importance of that and pleaded with South Africa to remove all obstacles hampering ease of movement and trade."

a1674.speaker: Thomas Thabane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a1674.speech: "South Africa's main concern is that our passport is easily accessible to foreign nationals who violate it by using it to enter South Africa to commit crime." ; "We assured South Africa that we were already working on improving our passport."

a1674.speaker: Basotho travellers and businesses
a1674.speech: As South Africa tightened border controls, thousands of Basotho complained that they were unable to travel out of the country, while businesses complained about the adverse effects the new controls were having on them.

a1674.speaker: Johnny Steinberg, writing for the Institute for Security Studies in 2005
a1674.speech: Put it this way: "[Lesotho's] citizens have always participated in the South African economy, and always will." He added, "[S]everal commentators have argued that the South African state has neither the capacity nor the moral authority to keep Lesotho's citizens out of South Africa; that border controls between the two countries are bound to whittle away, whether de jure or merely in practice; that the raison d'etre for Lesotho's sovereignty vanished at the end of Apartheid, and that political incorporation into South Africa is inevitable – or at very least, highly desirable – in the long run."

a1682.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (executive order of 4 February)
a1682.speech: Issued an executive order decreeing the withdrawal of the United States from organisations such as UNESCO and the UNHRC, and gave a deadline of 180 days for a review of the country's presence in and financing of all international intergovernmental organisations.

a1682.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1682.speech: Gave undignified treatment to President Zelensky, including calling him a dictator, at the White House meeting where an agreement to end the war was to be imposed on the Ukrainian president without his participation in the negotiations and without a security guarantee.

a1682.speaker: Certain observers (anonymous)
a1682.speech: Do not rule out the possibility of the United States leaving the IMF and the World Bank.

a1682.speaker: Project 2025 (document associated with Trump's candidacy)
a1682.speech: Explicitly reduces the IMF and the World Bank to the condition of expensive intermediaries that intercept American financing before it reaches projects abroad.

a1752.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1752.speech: Announced plans by the government to increase funding for Ghana's leading research centres, particularly in agriculture, health, and genetic medicine, to drive innovation and address key national challenges; said the government's decision was in response to growing concerns over the sustainability of critical research projects following the withdrawal of some international funding.

a1752.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1752.speech: Mentioned the West Africa Centre for Crop Improvement (WACCI), the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), and the West African Genetic Medicine Centre (WAGMC) as institutions whose work continues to contribute to solving both local and regional problems. "Ghana has been privileged to host some of the most impactful Centres of Excellence under the ACE Programme." He noted that these centres had made progress in improving food production, advancing health research, and tackling genetic disorders such as sickle cell disease.

a1752.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1752.speech: Spoke about the recent withdrawal of $156 million in funding from WACCBIP by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and disclosed that the government had stepped in to close the funding gap. "I personally assured the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ghana that we would make up for the loss of USAID funding from our own budget. I am pleased to report that the Ministry of Finance has fully provided for the $156 million that was pulled out, to enable the critical research to go ahead."

a1752.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1752.speech: Said Ghana must reduce its dependence on foreign aid to sustain its research institutions; while donor support remained important, he stressed the need for the government to take greater responsibility for funding innovation, especially in areas that directly affect the lives of Ghanaians.

a1752.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1752.speech: "Our innovation in these centres must have tangible impacts on the communities we serve. We must ensure that academic work aligns with national development priorities." He urged that research be localised so that its outcomes address the real needs of the people, particularly in agriculture and health.

a1752.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1752.speech: Called for stronger cooperation between universities, industry, and government agencies to make research results more applicable in real-world situations; said such partnerships would also help to mobilise resources and improve the sustainability of research centres in the country.

a1803.speaker: Professor Ntobeko Ntusi, CEO of the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC)
a1803.speech: Told GroundUp that "we were alerted on Thursday last week that the NIH is considering imminently terminating all grants to South Africa… many of us believe these are likely to be announced in the coming days" ; previously told Spotlight that US grants make up 28% of the SAMRC's funding.

a1803.speaker: University of Cape Town (UCT) (email to the health faculty)
a1803.speech: Warned on Sunday that while they still didn't have confirmation, "developments over the last two days indicate that the termination of US federal funding to South Africa appears to be imminent"; the email states that UCT has established a task team to "plan mitigation measures" if US-funded research projects are terminated.

a1803.speaker: Science Magazine
a1803.speech: Reported on Friday that the acting director of the NIH had sent an email to staff earlier that week asking them to compile a list of NIH grants for projects in South Africa; the email reportedly contained "similar wording" to a previous request for information about NIH grants related to transgender health and vaccine hesitancy.

a1803.speaker: Associate professor Sean Wasserman, infectious diseases, University of Cape Town
a1803.speech: Told GroundUp that at present the primary concern is that the grant could be cancelled at any moment; explained that the current treatment duration "keeps people in clinics and in contact with the healthcare system for a long time, which is a real cost to people. [For instance] It makes it difficult to maintain a job… And that also leads to treatment fatigue".

a1803.speaker: Associate professor Sean Wasserman, infectious diseases, University of Cape Town
a1803.speech: Said that although all the participants would still be able to get treatment in the ordinary health system in South Africa, they wouldn't necessarily be managed correctly: "They're on experimental drug regimens" ; "Transitioning them back to routine care is not ideal because the [experimental regimens] can have effects for weeks or months, which need to be monitored, which routine care isn't set up to do."

a1803.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (executive order of 7 February)
a1803.speech: States that the US would not provide "aid or assistance" to South Africa due to its alleged persecution of Afrikaans people and "racially disfavoured landowners".

a1803.speaker: US Secretary of State
a1803.speech: Over 80% of all USAID agreements have been terminated globally, according to the US Secretary of State.

a1857.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Government of Liberia, represented by the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP)
a1857.speech: On November 13, 2024, announced more than $114.4 million in funding for development initiatives designed to enhance economic growth by fostering reform and cultivating a healthy and educated workforce.

a1857.speaker: Mark Toner, U.S. Ambassador to Liberia
a1857.speech: Making remarks at the signing ceremony: "This additional investment is designed to support Liberian-led interventions in health, education, strategic reforms and market-driven inclusive economic growth. Through these funds, USAID programs help provide training for teachers, deliver health commodities to communities, and expand access to electricity in Liberia. By working together, the U.S. Government and the Government of Liberia aim to ensure that every dollar contributes to lasting, positive outcomes for the Liberian people."

a1857.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Minister of Finance of Liberia
a1857.speech: "America has always stood by our side as a strong partner in progress. We are grateful for your support and remain committed to working together," calling for a strengthened partnership to advance Liberia's agenda.

a1876.speaker: Issifou Moumouni, community relay in Kegamarou, Banikoara
a1876.speech: explained: "As you have just seen, I have already planned an educational talk session. And I, among the 200 households in my charge, have divided them into three. This means that each week I have three educational talks to give. During these talks, we speak with the population, raising their awareness of subjects of public interest. This is so that they can change their way of life. And that is how we have harmony in our community." According to him, specific themes are addressed during these talks: those linked to health or breastfeeding, making it possible to prevent any risk of malnutrition and serious cases of illness, especially for children.

a1876.speaker: Sano Afissou, community relay in Poto, Banikoara
a1876.speech: mentions the difficulties encountered during the group follow-ups, such as the lack of working equipment and logistical problems linked to the distance of households; he stresses the importance of collaboration among the relays and the help provided by the ASCQs in overcoming these obstacles: "Means of transport such as bicycles work well and facilitate their travel. The applications installed on the tablets also allow good synchronisation of the data collected in the field."

a1876.speaker: Sabé Basé Ayou, Qualified Community Health Agent (ASCQ) and basic nurse, Sompérékou district
a1876.speech: explains: "My main role consists of ensuring that the relays correctly carry out their home visits to detect and manage cases of illness, mainly among children under five. In the event of an illness requiring more advanced care, patients must be directed to a health centre. Each month, these group follow-ups are organised to take stock of community health activities by involving the various relays concerned." He manages a network of 46 relays and strives to supervise them regularly while planning educational sessions.

a1876.speaker: Noélie Guézo, in charge of community health at UNICEF Parakou
a1876.speech: announces that UNICEF plays an essential role in supporting the programme, in collaboration with various donors and technical partners, and indicates that the organisation's participation in the training and equipping of community relays constitutes a crucial contribution to disease prevention: "These community relays, identified within the population, focus on protecting children's rights and fight against early marriages through these awareness-raising activities and educational talks." ; "Thanks to awareness-raising and education on hygiene, we have managed to obtain positive results in managing these health problems. Indeed, UNICEF's commitment to implementing the National Community Health Policy, validated by the Beninese government in 2020, has enabled the organisation to support six pilot communes and has since extended its action to eighteen communes, including Borgou and Alibori. This support, which is provided in collaboration with other partners, aims to improve the coordination of interventions and the drafting of strategic documents. UNICEF has also contributed to identifying and strengthening the capacities of community relays, who are trained by their own communities. These relays are equipped with essential material for their work, such as bicycles, tablets and malnutrition screening kits. Above the relays, the Qualified Community Health Agents supervise their work and ensure their continuing training." ; She explains that the relays and the community health agents play a crucial role in health promotion although they are not authorised to distribute medicines: "Their mission focuses on education and prevention, while medical care is provided by qualified professionals."

a1876.speaker: Dr Mohamed Orou Yari, Coordinator of the Banikoara health zone
a1876.speech: shared encouraging results regarding the implementation since 2023 of the new National Community Health Policy, which he said has led to a significant drop in malaria cases and a rise in antenatal consultations and vaccination coverage, with notable results such as a decrease of 21,000 malaria cases in six months and malaria falling to the third leading cause of consultation in 2024: "The model, launched in six pilot communes, rests on the engagement of communities and the intervention of community relays for health promotion." He also underlined persistent challenges, notably the need for incentives for the relays, sustainable funding and ownership by the population, saying that collaboration with local elected officials and effective coordination with integrated health policies are essential, and that the full success of the policy will depend on continued engagement and regular evaluation to guarantee accessible and effective health services.

a1988.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (statement sent to the newsroom)
a1988.speech: According to a statement sent to our newsroom, the signing of the Financing Agreement between the governments of Mozambique and the United States, through the MCC, is scheduled for September this year in Washington DC.

a2326.speaker: United States Embassy in Mozambique (statement)
a2326.speech: Announced that, following the Foreign Assistance Review, the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) Board of Directors met in August and recommended moving forward with Mozambique's Coastal Connectivity and Resilience Compact, a recommendation reflecting continued confidence in cooperation between the United States and Mozambique; said the Compact is fully aligned with U.S. foreign policy priorities and that the refinements underscore the U.S. government's commitment to accountability, transparency, and measurable results.

a2326.speaker: Abigail L. Dressel, U.S. Charge d'Affaires in Mozambique
a2326.speech: "The United States is proud of our longstanding cooperation with Mozambique. The decision to move forward with the Compact demonstrates the commitment of both countries to building a stronger and more prosperous future. By refining the program's focus, we are ensuring that American investment creates opportunities for Mozambicans while promoting stability and economic growth that benefit both our nations."

a2466.speaker: CHADEMA deputy chairperson (Tanzania Mainland)
a2466.speech: Revealed Tuesday that a single donor stepped forward as he collected the candidacy forms at CHADEMA headquarters in Mikocheni, Dar es Salaam.

a2466.speaker: Tundu Lissu, Tanzanian opposition figure (CHADEMA)
a2466.speech: "The Sh1.5 million required to pay for these forms has been provided by one of our members named Edgar Edson Mwakabela, popularly known as Sativa" ; "He called me and said, 'I want to pay for that form because I believe that if you become the chairperson of this party, you will carry out the work that needs to be done in this country, which is fighting for the rights of Tanzanians and advocating for a new Tanzania that ensures we are not abducted or disappeared" ; Lissu went on to reveal that Sativa, who was shot in the head after his abduction on June 23, 2024, had fled the country in fear for his life.

a2466.speaker: Edgar Mwakabela ('Sativa'), abduction survivor
a2466.speech: In his recount of his abduction, Mwakabela says he was taken to various police stations in Dar es Salaam and Arusha by his abductors, whom he alleges were police officers.

a2466.speaker: Tanzanian Police
a2466.speech: Despite naming an individual he was able to identify during his ordeal, the police have suggested there might be some "distorted facts."

a2466.speaker: Tundu Lissu, Tanzanian opposition figure (CHADEMA)
a2466.speech: Regarding his assassination attempt, Lissu has been accusing the current Arusha Regional Commissioner, Paul Makonda, of being involved in the effort by plotting and leading a team of assassins to Dodoma: "It was Paul Makonda who led the Task Force" ; "He was staying at the African Dream Hotel, which is why he wasn't present at the State House event that day. Among those who need to be criminally investigated regarding my allegations is Paul Makonda. Even the two young men who shot me are still out there; when the time comes, we will name them." ; While Lissu insists his allegations are based on credible sources, he has also questioned the unusual circumstances surrounding the Regional Commissioner's absence from a historical event presided over by the President at the State House in Dar es Salaam.

a2466.speaker: Paul Makonda, Arusha Regional Commissioner
a2466.speech: When asked by reporters on November 17, 2024, about Lissu's accusations, he refuted them, arguing that they were political statements with no basis in truth: "There is no truth to it. If the people at Clouds [Media] were to look back and recall their records, they would remember that on the very day the incident occurred, I was in Dar es Salaam at Mnazi Mmoja grounds. We were holding a free medical check-up campaign, so I wasn't even at the scene of the incident" ; Makonda suggested that Lissu was using him as a political scapegoat, saying: "Do the math. Someone was attacked years ago, then came back to Tanzania and even ran for the presidency. Have you ever heard them mention Makonda? After losing the presidency, he left and returned to his home. Now, he has come back and suddenly started mentioning Makonda in 2024. When you see how this thing is developing, it's clearly a political issue."

a2765.speaker: Sengi Dadhi, social and resettlement management team leader at the Ethiopian Roads Administration (ERA)
a2765.speech: Disclosed that the World Bank asked for assessments on all four lots: "The request included preparing a livelihood restoration plan."

a2765.speaker: Sengi Dadhi, social and resettlement management team leader at the Ethiopian Roads Administration (ERA)
a2765.speech: Said the ERA plans to start paying out compensations right after the release of funds by the World Bank and finalise in April 2023: "However, compensating the households could take up to two years." ; "The money is used to contribute to the well-being of the households sustainably."

a2765.speaker: Environmental and social impact assessment / consultant's report (Zelalem Temesgen)
a2765.speech: Revealed that close to 1,000 rural agricultural households in 15 kebeles along the 93Km have been impacted, and that the productivity of these households, comprising 12,500 people in Adami Tulu, Dugda and Arsi Negele weredas, has dropped by half due to the expressway's altering of farming and pastoralist activities; the report also revealed that the majority of owners who surrendered property for the Modjo to Batu segment had expressed dissatisfaction with their payments, claiming the compensation was insufficient. An earlier assessment estimated the total number of households affected by the entire project at 3,457.

a2765.speaker: Warso Eilemo, 55-year-old farmer affected by the road project
a2765.speech: "Flooding hadn't been a problem before the road project." ; On the 230,000 Br he received as compensation for one hectare ceded to the road project two years ago: "It wasn't enough to cover the losses I incurred."

a2765.speaker: Officials (Ethiopian Roads Administration)
a2765.speech: Say they expect the financing will be approved in the coming months; estimate 109 million Br is enough to cover the proposed livelihood restoration project costs, and believe that compensating based on cash cannot address the issues unless sustainable livelihood schemes and training support them, so the money will not be paid out to beneficiaries in cash.

a2765.speaker: Yonas Jarsa, independent legal consultant and former legal officer at the central bank
a2765.speech: Sees conducting a need assessment and compensating households as complex, noting that Ethiopia has no legal framework to determine eligibility or the amount of compensation for losses due to development projects, compensation being based on a law governing the expropriation of land holdings introduced in 2005 and amended in 2019: "However, efforts should be made to negotiate and allocate the highest budget possible."

a2815.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian President
a2815.speech: Has accused Russia of creating a misleading image of peace by announcing a ceasefire while still carrying out military operations in parts of Ukraine ; speaking in a televised address, expressed his deep concern over what he described as a calculated attempt by Moscow to deceive the international community ; said Russia's announcement of a ceasefire was more of a public relations maneuver rather than a genuine effort to stop the bloodshed and destruction in Ukraine ; said that while Russian officials claim to be observing a temporary halt in fighting, their forces continue to launch attacks in several regions ; cited ongoing shelling in eastern and southern Ukraine, noting that these acts contradict the spirit and intention of a true ceasefire ; emphasized that genuine peace cannot coexist with simultaneous acts of violence, especially when civilians remain at risk ; described the so-called ceasefire as a “performance,” orchestrated to create the illusion of responsibility and restraint ; warned that while the world is being shown one picture, the reality on the ground in Ukraine is far more brutal and unforgiving.

a2815.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian President
a2815.speech: Urged the international community not to be misled by Russia's narrative and to pay closer attention to what is happening on the ground ; said the difference between words and actions is vast, and it is the actions—particularly those that result in death and destruction—that must be judged.

a2815.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian President
a2815.speech: Said that any genuine efforts toward peace must begin with full transparency and accountability from both sides, particularly from Russia, which he says has broken ceasefire promises in the past ; further stated that Ukraine remains committed to the pursuit of peace but will not compromise its sovereignty or security in the face of what he termed “staged diplomacy.”

a2815.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian President
a2815.speech: Appealed to allies and international organizations to continue supporting Ukraine not only with words but with actions that will help protect Ukrainian lives and defend the country's territorial integrity ; also called for increased humanitarian assistance in areas still under attack, highlighting the dire situation of families trapped by ongoing Russian bombardments.

a2815.speaker: Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukrainian President
a2815.speech: Acknowledged the spiritual significance of the Easter season but said true Easter blessings can only come when aggression ceases and lives are no longer in peril ; closed his speech with a message of resilience, telling Ukrainians that truth and justice will ultimately prevail over deception and violence.

a2815.speaker: Many international observers
a2815.speech: Have echoed Zelensky's sentiments, noting that Russia has previously used religious or diplomatic occasions to make ceasefire announcements that were not fully upheld.

a2815.speaker: Human rights groups
a2815.speech: In response to Zelensky's speech, have called for independent monitoring of the ceasefire to verify whether violations are taking place ; they argue that only through rigorous observation and reporting can the international community hold violators accountable and ensure civilian safety.

a3089.speaker: Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila, Prime Minister of Namibia
a3089.speech: Revealed during the 9th Session of the Africa Regional Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction Conference that of the planned N$1.6 billion drought relief programme, the government is currently facing a funding gap of about N$482 million to reach an additional 373 276 households, which translates into 1.26 million people, or 41% of the country's population ; "Therefore, the government is appealing for assistance. Positive responses to our appeal for assistance have been received from development partners, for which we are grateful. Assistance comes in the form of cash and in-kind donations of food and equipment made directly to the government, and donations in cash and kind made through UN agencies. The SADC region is currently going through one of the worst droughts in recent years, induced by the El Niño phenomenon." ; "This situation resulted in the threatened lives and livelihoods for about 58 million people, with food and water security severely compromised. This led to most member states declaring a state of disaster on account of drought. The region subsequently launched a joint appeal for assistance to supplement their national responses."

a3089.speaker: Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila, Prime Minister of Namibia
a3089.speech: Added that at the continental level the situation around climate change is worsening and continues to become unpredictable for most countries, which she said calls for better preparedness and progressive policy interventions ; "Africa is on the frontline of the climate crisis and faces a multitude of disasters, from relentless climate extremes to environmental degradation. Of late, the continent has witnessed severe disasters, including tropical cyclones, floods, droughts and veld fires, which have resulted in significant economic losses, displacement of livelihoods, and the loss of precious lives."

a3089.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a3089.speech: In May declared a state of emergency on the protracted drought, which has seen the country's aggregated cereal production of white maize, sorghum, pearl millet and wheat decreasing by 53%, while dam levels countrywide have dropped by 69.7%.

a3089.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), July/September 2024 report
a3089.speech: Stated that about 1.15 million people, which is 38% of the country's population, were classified in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis) or above, necessitating urgent humanitarian assistance to mitigate food consumption gaps and protect livelihoods; attributes the ongoing crisis to several key factors, including climate shocks, particularly the impact of El Niño, which has led to erratic rainfall and prolonged drought, and highlights deteriorating livestock conditions; warned that national food levels are critically low, with silos holding just 15% of their total capacity as of June 2024.

a3089.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report (recommendations)
a3089.speech: Made various key recommendations to improve food availability, which included providing drought-resistant seeds and modern agricultural training to communal farmers, increasing capacity-building initiatives for agricultural extension officers, and expanding hydroponic fodder production across all regions; it likewise recommended that the government continues monitoring key factors such as staple commodity prices, inflation impacts, seasonal rainfall patterns and the potential effects of La Niña.

a3100.speaker: Fatima Ali, community mobilizer with UNFPA in Maiduguri, Borno State, flood survivor
a3100.speech: “The water reached up to our chests” ... “We kept walking for two hours through the flooded roads.” ; “It happened two weeks before my expected delivery date. Because I am pregnant, I couldn’t walk on my own. It was my husband who helped me move through the water.”

a3100.speaker: Fatima Ali, community mobilizer with UNFPA
a3100.speech: “even with the flood, I still go to work. The reason is that I want to encourage other women.” ; “The work that UNFPA does, we prioritize maternal health above all… And when I give birth, I will be more passionate about helping women, having had firsthand experience of what motherhood is like.”

a3100.speaker: Data from flood-hit countries such as Cameroon (cited)
a3100.speech: shows an increased risk of early and forced marriage and intimate partner violence.

a3100.speaker: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of UNFPA
a3100.speech: According to the report, more than 14,000 displaced people have received information about sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence and the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse. Over 1,500 dignity kits containing essential hygiene supplies including menstrual pads, underwear and soap have been distributed in flood-affected areas.

a3100.speaker: Mustapha Hussein, digital literacy facilitator with UNFPA in Maiduguri
a3100.speech: “As a humanitarian worker, it is not easy providing assistance for the affected population when you are also affected.” ; “Almost all of our community was submerged by floods.” ; “To trek from here for 7 km to the camp was not easy. And then it was also terrible and scary.” ; “Now I am recovering and bouncing back.” ; “My next line of action is to start building my home from scratch.” ; “As a humanitarian worker and someone that grew up in a complex emergency situation, this flood hasn’t hindered me.”

a3310.speaker: Kelvin Chibomba, policy analyst
a3310.speech: Has called on Government through the Ministry of Tourism and Arts to implement robust policies that are going to help the sector to thrive ; said Government should put in place policies that are going to attract tourists as the sector has the ability to be one of the major foreign export earners for the country ; said it is prudent that the country develops policies that drive towards promoting tourist attraction which will be cardinal for the growth of the sector ; added that the ministry needs to identify gaps in the sector and cement them as this will be critical for the revenue generation ; said the country has not widely promoted the tourism sector which has negatively affected its growth thereby denying the treasury the much-needed revenue ; said it is vital to ensure that the sector is promoted globally as this will unlock its potential.

a3555.speaker: Botswana Climate Change Network (BCCN)
a3555.speech: Has voiced deep concerns about the impact of the US decision to halt financial aid for global climate initiatives on the country’s energy sector and sustainable development.

a3555.speaker: Tshepiso Masilonyana, Programme Officer of the Botswana Climate Change Network
a3555.speech: Warned that halting USAID support will seriously hinder Botswana’s ability to combat energy poverty and develop innovative, sustainable solutions to climate challenges: “The Trump administration’s decision to freeze USAID funding is a huge blow to renewable energy efforts across Africa, particularly in Botswana. The Power Africa initiative, which has been a key driver of renewable energy projects in Botswana, now faces major uncertainty.” ; warned both the mega solar project and the Roof Top Solar project now face serious risks due to funding shortages and loss of technical assistance: “The mega solar project, one of Africa’s most ambitious renewable energy initiatives, was set to generate up to 5,000 megawatts of electricity in Botswana and Namibia. It was a collaborative effort involving USAID Power Africa, the governments of Botswana and Namibia, the African Development Bank, and other stakeholders. This initiative aimed to position Botswana as a regional hub for solar energy, supplying clean power domestically and exporting surplus to the Southern Africa Power Pool (SAPP).”

a3555.speaker: Tshepiso Masilonyana, Programme Officer of the Botswana Climate Change Network
a3555.speech: Described the US exit from the Paris Agreement as a “serious setback” for countries like Botswana: “As a civil society organisation committed to climate justice, we are deeply concerned about the implications of this decision. For African nations, climate change is not a distant threat; it is a present and worsening crisis.” ; “The US withdrawal is not just abdication of responsibility; it is a betrayal of the people whose lives are most at risk.” ; “This decision sets a dangerous precedent, encouraging other major polluters to deprioritise their climate commitments and reversing years of progress.” ; “Africa contributes less than 4% of global emissions, and Botswana less than 0.1%, yet our continent faces the harshest consequences of climate change. The US, which is responsible for 17% of global emissions, walking away from the Paris Agreement undermines Africa’s ability to mitigate the damage caused by pollution we did not create.” He also pointed out that while the Paris Agreement is not perfect, it represents a global commitment to reducing emissions and supporting adaptation efforts in developing nations.

a3555.speaker: Tshepiso Masilonyana, Programme Officer of the Botswana Climate Change Network
a3555.speech: Urged African leaders to remain committed to their climate goals and seek alternative funding.

a3649.speaker: Dennis W. Hearne, U.S. Ambassador to Mozambique
a3649.speech: “MCC investments are designed to reduce poverty through economic growth. This process presents an invaluable opportunity to build trust around public investment and government efficacy. Ultimately, Mozambique's second MCC Compact has the potential to catalyse transformational development in Mozambique.”

a3649.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Mozambique
a3649.speech: Announced in December 2020 that this second MCC compact in Mozambique will focus on improving agriculture and rural transport, two national priorities identified by the Government of the Republic of Mozambique.

a3649.speaker: Government of Mozambique
a3649.speech: Identified that Mozambique's second compact would focus on Zambezia Province, which has the potential for greater agricultural production and to reduce poverty.

a3829.speaker: Dieudonné Dukundane, Executive Secretary of the Central Corridor
a3829.speech: Declared at a press conference on Tuesday 31 October, following the signature of the project agreement: « The development of transport infrastructure on Lake Tanganyika, once completed, will reduce by 40% the total cost of goods transiting through the central corridor » ; noted that goods using the central corridor reach 15 million tonnes a year and that «only 20% of these goods transit by the lake route. The rest takes the Dar Es Salaam-Kobero-Bujumbura road route, which is longer and more expensive» ; explained this situation by the fact that the railway linking the port of Dar-Es-Salaam to the port of Kigoma was damaged over the last twelve years and was rehabilitated this year ; stressed that developing trade by rail and by lake requires appropriate infrastructure, notably trains, boats and well-equipped ports able to receive large vessels, concluding: « Transport infrastructure constitutes a lever of development. »

a3829.speaker: Libérat Mfumukeko, Executive Secretary of the East African Community (EAC)
a3829.speech: Makes it known that this financing constitutes the second phase of the project, the first having been carried out around Lake Victoria for an amount of 700 million dollars: «The infrastructure was improved appreciably.»

a3829.speaker: Nestor Sindayigaya, foodstuffs importer
a3829.speech: Considers that « the rehabilitation of the Dar-Es-Salaam-Kigoma railway and the improvement of transport infrastructure on Lake Tanganyika will not be enough to facilitate trade » ; says importers need facilitation, if not simplification, of the customs clearance process on the Tanzanian side: « Customs clearance of goods is easier at the port of Mombasa than at that of Dar Es Salaam. That pushes importers to route their goods through the northern corridor, which is expensive. » ; notes that lake transport requires sufficient capital, that is, having several containers of goods to fill the boat, hence the use of the road route.

a3829.speaker: Gilbert Niyongabo, professor of economic sciences at the University of Burundi
a3829.speech: Maintains that the rehabilitation of the Dar-Es-Salaam-Kigoma railway constitutes the future of trade in the region: « The railway is faster than the road and presents fewer accidents. Wagons transport far more goods than trucks. » ; notes that on the road route trucks make several stops, « At least eight stops on Tanzanian soil, whereas current trade policy urges one stop per border. This increases transport costs. » ; indicates that Burundian importers using the central corridor have two options: « The first is the Dar-Es-Salaam-Kobero-Bujumbura road route », which he signals is the longest (about 1,600 km) and the most costly, and the second is the Dar-Es-Salaam-Kigoma railway followed by a lake route linking the port of Kigoma to that of Bujumbura.

a3829.speaker: Economic operators (unnamed)
a3829.speech: Remain doubtful about the World Bank’s USD 600 million investment in improving transport infrastructure on Lake Tanganyika.

a3907.speaker: Nigerian federal government
a3907.speech: RUGA Settlement, according to the federal government, seeks to assist pastoral families; animal farmers, not just cattle herders, to settle in an organized place with provision of necessary and adequate basic amenities such as schools, hospitals, road networks, veterinary clinics, markets and manufacturing entities that will process and add value to meats and animal products.

a3907.speaker: DAWN Commission
a3907.speech: Proposes the revisit of the abandoned ranching project, amid recent concerns by the populace of southwest Nigeria.

a3907.speaker: Mercy Corps (NGO report in May)
a3907.speech: Clashes between nomadic herders and farmers have claimed roughly 7,000 lives over the past five years and cost the Nigerian economy $13 billion (11.57 billion euros) annually.

a3907.speaker: FAO
a3907.speech: Puts the minimum daily requirement of animal protein at 35g daily.

a3907.speaker: Nigerian government estimates
a3907.speech: Nigeria consumes 360,000 tonnes of beef each year, accounting for half of all consumption in West Africa.

a4010.speaker: The Kremlin
a4010.speech: Announced that among the most notable agreements signed was a strategic partnership on the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

a4010.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a4010.speech: Declared: “Our trade exchanges are still modest, but they are progressing,” underlining the potential for collaboration in the fields of geology, natural resources, energy, logistics and humanitarian aid.

a4010.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a4010.speech: At the Russia–Africa summit in Saint Petersburg on 27 and 28 July 2023, designated Mali as a key partner in Africa, praising Bamako’s determination to preserve its strategic independence.

a4010.speaker: General Assimi Goïta, President of the Malian transition
a4010.speech: Hailed “the excellence of the cooperation with the Russian Federation”, highlighting “the mutual trust and efficiency” that characterise this relationship.

a4010.speaker: Wikipedia (cited source)
a4010.speech: According to Wikipedia, nuclear energy is used mainly to produce electricity on a massive and continuous basis, and is also used in other fields such as naval and space propulsion, desalination of seawater, district heating and various industrial and even medical applications, notably in radiotherapy and medical imaging.

a4033.speaker: European Commission internal draft document (seen by POLITICO)
a4033.speech: Links the EU's help for poorer countries to concrete results in preventing people coming to the bloc, and suggests potentially cutting funds to poorer countries if they don't play their part in reducing migration flows: "It shall combine all appropriate tools and the necessary leverage through a flexible incitative approach with, as appropriate within this context, possible changes in [the] allocation of funding related to migration." ; "Increased coherence between migration, asylum and external policies is needed to ensure that the Union's external assistance supports partner countries to manage migration more effectively."

a4033.speaker: European Commission internal draft document (seen by POLITICO)
a4033.speech: States that aid programs will be lumped into a single Global Europe Fund subdivided into six geographic categories, with figures omitted, and that a separate, undefined money pot will cater for Ukraine from 2028 to 2034: "The Instrument should provide the framework for assistance for the fast recovery, reconstruction and modernization of the country."

a4098.speaker: Reserve Bank of Malawi (Financial and Economic Review for Q2 2025)
a4098.speech: Data show that total revenues for the quarter from April 1 to June 30 stood at K1.1 trillion against expenditures at K2.3 trillion, creating a K1.2 trillion deficit. Reads part of the report: “Total revenues during 2025Q2 were estimated at K1.1 trillion. This represented a 14.2 percent increase from K974 billion recorded during the preceding quarter and a 17.1 percent growth from K949.9 billion collected in a corresponding quarter of 2024. The outturn followed an 8.2 percent rise in tax revenue collections to K895.1 billion, a 47 percent increase in grant collections to K190.9 billion and a 59.5 percent expansion in non-tax revenues to K26.4 billion.”

a4098.speaker: Reserve Bank of Malawi
a4098.speech: Has attributed the rise in the budget deficit to the decline in both tax and non-tax revenues and some expenditure pressure which intensified in May.

a4098.speaker: Booker Matemvu, economic consultant
a4098.speech: Said the situation risks the projected budget deficit to balloon while threatening the public debt to continue piling which could result in economic recession if not handled properly: “This means that the government is spending more than it is collecting. Essentially this leads to continued borrowing on the local and foreign markets to finance the insatiable appetite to spending. It also calls to question the budget deficit assumptions in the budget.” ; said if the deficit figures are off sharply like “we have observed above, it means fiscal discipline is off course and the economy, if not treated quickly, might be heading to a recession”.

a4098.speaker: Bertha Bangara-Chikadza, acting president of the Economics Association of Malawi
a4098.speech: Said the current trends in the budget deficit indicate that government spending is consistently outpacing revenue, creating an unsustainable financial situation: “If this trend continues, Malawi risks not only exceeding its annual deficit target, but also exacerbating inflation and deepening its debt crisis. It is worth noting, however, that higher deficits during election years are not uncommon. Historical data reveals that deficits in election years have averaged over 70 percent higher than those in non-election years, highlighting the cyclical nature of fiscal pressures during such periods.”

a4098.speaker: Agnes Nyirongo, economic governance officer at the Centre for Social Concern
a4098.speech: Said huge recurrent expenditure and low development expenditure threatens to derail long-term poverty reduction efforts: “If we continue increasing recurrent costs, largely salaries and administrative overheads while cutting investments in health, education and infrastructure, we are simply locking ourselves into a low-growth, high-inequality future.”

a4098.speaker: Alick Nyasulu, economic statistician
a4098.speech: Is quoted as having cautioned that rising government deficits coupled with the foreign aid and debt squeeze, will force the government to borrow more from the domestic market.

a4098.speaker: Treasury (Malawi)
a4098.speech: Projected that the fiscal deficit will be primarily financed through domestic borrowing amounting to K2.33 trillion and foreign borrowing of K145.78 billion.

a4303.speaker: Mathurin Nago, President of the National Assembly of Benin
a4303.speech: Reports that, following the Head of State, 50 deputies requested the opening of the present extraordinary session, covering the designation of National Assembly representatives at polling stations, amendments to the Electoral Code, and bills on the statutes of Customs officers, National Police personnel, Water, Forest and Hunting officers, the Civil Service, retirement pensions, the bar, Supreme Court magistrates, and the private practice of medical and paramedical professions.

a4303.speaker: Mathurin Nago, President of the National Assembly of Benin
a4303.speech: Invited the deputies to show availability in order to tackle these files, stressing that Parliament will show ingenuity in examining the maximum number of files during these fifteen days.

a4303.speaker: Mathurin Nago, President of the National Assembly of Benin
a4303.speech: Denounced the start of certain works before ratification of the agreement, saying this way of doing things is a violation of the texts, which prescribe that agreements be ratified by the National Assembly before their execution on the ground; stressed that since the 6th legislature, more than 700 billion CFA francs of financing agreements have been authorised by the National Assembly.

a4303.speaker: Deputies who spoke in the general debate
a4303.speech: Hailed the government’s efforts for road development, but invited the Executive to review road maintenance so as to avoid having to redo the same roads each time.

a4303.speaker: Bani Samari and Eric Houndété, deputies
a4303.speech: Were worried by the interest rate of the second project, finding the rate of 10% exorbitant ; Bani Samari: “It is true that we must develop, but not at any price.”

a4303.speaker: André Okounlola, deputy
a4303.speech: Wanted to know the state of the Kétou-Savè file, which the government had announced as completed, and was concerned about what is blocking the start of work on the Tovègbamè bridge at Adjohoun, whose financing agreement has been ratified by the National Assembly for two years.

a4303.speaker: Gustave Sonon, Minister in charge of Relations with Institutions
a4303.speech: Defended the two files (the ISTISNA’A loan agreement and the EBID loan for the Parakou-Djougou road) before the National Assembly, in the presence of his colleague in charge of Justice, Valentin Djénontin.

a4530.speaker: Stella Ojulowo, 48, farmer in Oroto, Ilaje (Ondo State)
a4530.speech: “Before now, I planted crops that we would harvest, eat, and still sell the rest for money. But now, nothing nothing.” ; “I no feel better o.” ; recalled that in 2015 a sea incursion brought a strange transformation to her modest maize farm, the ears of corn curling and yellowing and eventually drying up, and that since then much of her farmland has been swallowed by the sea, forcing her into fish trading ; remembers when the intrusion first became noticeable, about a decade ago.

a4530.speaker: USAID
a4530.speech: According to USAID, at least 41 million Nigerians, about 24 per cent of the population, live in areas severely threatened by climate change.

a4530.speaker: Yinusa Asiwaju-Bello, professor of applied geology and marine science at the Federal University of Technology, Akure (FUTA)
a4530.speech: Explains that as seawater pushes further inland, it mingles with freshwater sources, devastating the ecosystem: “The sea has been aggressive and trying to come inland and take over” ; said one of the major devastations is the loss of agricultural productivity because “When the saltwater enters the freshwater, it kills the food crops.”

a4530.speaker: A 2019 study published on ScienceDirect
a4530.speech: Describes saltwater intrusion as the inland advancement of seawater into freshwater aquifers and surface water bodies, disrupting ecosystems and agricultural productivity, particularly in coastal regions like Ilaje.

a4530.speaker: Abike Olugbuyi, widow and farmer-turned-fishmonger in Araromi Waterside
a4530.speech: Said that when the sea encroached and destroyed her crops, she wept for weeks, and that she pivoted to fishmongering: “Now, I deal with fish processing.” ; claims that food prices have doubled and access to affordable staples is severely limited.

a4530.speaker: Adenike Mesagan, 58-year-old farmer in Araromi Waterside
a4530.speech: Said the saltwater has devastated not just their farms, but their lives, even emptied their plates as a people: “We travel all the way to Igbokoda to buy raw food.”

a4530.speaker: Locals in Ilaje
a4530.speech: Blame oil exploration for the intrusion, suspecting that drilling and extraction may be accelerating the contamination of freshwater by saltwater.

a4530.speaker: A 2025 study by Omorede Odigie and Nosa Obayagbona, environmental management and toxicology researchers at the University of Benin
a4530.speech: Finds that excessive groundwater extraction, climate change-related sea level rise and oil and gas exploration are the main contributing factors to the surge of saltwater.

a4530.speaker: Caleb Omoteinse, retired fisherman turned small-scale farmer
a4530.speech: “We’re not the ones producing the food we consume.” ; “We still do small-scale farming of maize and cassava. On dry land currently. But once the sea incursion starts, it destroys everything…around every rainy June.” ; “The problem is bigger than us.” ; “We are helpless.”

a4530.speaker: Ogechi Okebugwu, programme coordinator of the Small Scale Women Farmers Organisation in Nigeria
a4530.speech: Said that when agriculture declines, the locals, especially women, face increased burdens: “Women lose the ability to feed their families, to sell produce in the local market and increase their financial dependence on men, reducing economic agency”; adding that another consequence of the farming crisis is child labour and malnutrition.

a4530.speaker: Yinusa Asiwaju-Bello, professor of applied geology and marine science at FUTA
a4530.speech: Noted that freshwater species are dying out, unable to survive the increased salinity, and that marine fish are moving closer inland while native freshwater fish are disappearing; “The entire existence of the Ilaje people is under threat.”

a4530.speaker: A 2019 environmental study in coastal Ondo
a4530.speech: Found a combined loss of nearly six per cent in fish species, decapod crustaceans, and vascular plants, due largely to saltwater intrusion.

a4530.speaker: Adenike Mesagan, 58-year-old farmer in Araromi Waterside
a4530.speech: Said there are months, between June and September, when fish simply die in the creeks: “We can’t use our water to bathe, cook, or wash our clothes.”

a4530.speaker: Residents of Ilaje
a4530.speech: Say they feel abandoned; they had high hopes for Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa, an Ilaje man, who has now been in office for two years, but claimed that little has changed; complain that while the state has hosted tourism events on Araromi Beach, little has been done to address their suffering.

a4530.speaker: Mr Olugbuyi, Araromi resident
a4530.speech: “The governor just comes here for the beach.”

a4530.speaker: Caleb Omoteinse, retired fisherman turned small-scale farmer
a4530.speech: “We are far from the government.”

a4530.speaker: Rotimi Akinsola, senior special adviser on Agriculture and Agribusiness to Governor Aiyedatiwa
a4530.speech: Acknowledged that communities like Ilaje have long been neglected, but said the current administration is working to ensure they are now being prioritised; noted that addressing saltwater intrusion falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government: “It is under the Niger Delta Development… All we can do for our citizens is to ensure they farm in a good place, move them to where they can farm.” ; “We can move the farmers to dry land and give them fertilisers so they can plant”, adding that the government has set up the Ondo State Empowerment Centre to train farmers on various farming strategies, including soilless farming ; “Those who come here, we give what we can. Recently, some women applied for land, and we have asked them to come for a meeting.”

a4530.speaker: Ondo State government
a4530.speech: Announced in February that it had “concluded plans” to provide farm clusters and 1,000 hectares of land for farmers in the state, particularly those affected by coastal erosion.

a4530.speaker: Media reports
a4530.speech: Indicate that over 100 women and youths were trained in March.

a4530.speaker: Women in Ilaje who spoke with Premium Times
a4530.speech: Said they were unaware of any such government initiatives.

a4530.speaker: Residents, particularly farmers, who spoke with Premium Times
a4530.speech: Said they have seen no tangible agricultural support, despite the ₦33 billion budget the Ondo State Oil Producing Areas Development Commission (OSOPADEC) received this year to support social and infrastructural development in Ilaje and Ese-Odo.

a4530.speaker: Folorunsho Adetayo, associate professor of marine geophysics at FUTA
